pages.x: Rome had ruled Judea since 63 BC, first through kings such as Herod the Great, who rebuilt the Temple in Jerusalem in splendour, then through governors. Taxes, insults to the Jewish faith and quarrels between Jews and Greeks built up, and in 66, when the governor took money from the Temple treasury, Jerusalem rose.

Nero sent his general Vespasian with three legions, and he took Galilee town by town. A rebel commander there, Joseph ben Matityahu, surrendered and foretold that Vespasian would be emperor. When that came true in 69, Joseph, now Flavius Josephus, became the historian of the war.

In 70 Vespasian's son Titus besieged Jerusalem, crowded with pilgrims for Passover and split between rebel groups who fought each other. Famine set in. In the summer the Romans broke through the walls, and the Temple went up in flames.

Josephus says over a million died in the siege, surely too many, and 97,000 were taken as slaves. The Temple was never rebuilt. Jews still mourn it on the fast of Tisha B'Av, and the Western Wall, part of its platform, is the holiest place where Jews pray.

In Rome, an arch built in honour of Titus shows his soldiers carrying off the treasures of the Temple, among them its great seven-branched lampstand, the menorah. That menorah is now the emblem of the State of Israel.

The last rebels held Masada, a fortress on a cliff top by the Dead Sea. In 73 or 74 the Romans built a huge ramp up to its walls. Josephus says that when they broke in, they found that the 960 defenders had killed themselves rather than be taken. Archaeologists still argue over his account.

In 132, after the emperor Hadrian planned a Roman city on the ruins of Jerusalem, Simon bar Kosiba led a new revolt. His followers called him Bar Kokhba, son of the star. For three years he ruled a free Judea and struck his own coins, until Rome crushed the revolt.

Hadrian built his city, Aelia Capitolina, and banned Jews from it. He renamed the province Syria Palaestina. The historian Cassius Dio says 580,000 Jewish fighters were killed and 985 villages destroyed.

The wars ended Jewish self-rule in the land for almost 1,900 years. They also changed Judaism: without its Temple, it came to centre on scripture, the synagogue and the study of the rabbis, a faith that could be carried anywhere in the world.
pts: The Temple of Jerusalem destroyed in AD 70
Judaism lived on without its Temple
